newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-PROS REMEMBER BEN HOGAN FOR COMPETITIVENESS AND IMPACT.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-PROS REMEMBER BEN HOGAN FOR COMPETITIVENESS AND IMPACT.

text.p: Professional golfers on the PGA and Senior tours remember Ben Hogan, who died Friday three weeks before his 85th birthday, for his competitiveness and his lasting impact on their game -- and as perhaps the best who ever played.
Jack Nicklaus was playing in a skins game in British Columbia, Canada, when he learned of Hogan's death.

"Ben was a very private person who loved the game and its competition," said Nicklaus. "I remember playing two rounds with him at the 1960 U.S. Open. I was amazed at his concentration, as well as his shotmaking and total commitment to perfection.

"I always liked Ben. He treated me as an equal and I was very flattered when he sought me out to play at certain events. Golf has lost, in my opinion, the best shot-maker the game has ever seen. We will all miss him very much -- he was a great man," said Nicklaus.
At the Franklin Quest championship in Park City, Utah, several senior players commented on Hogan's passing, including Johnny Miller, making his senior debut.

"He had a great influence on my life. I sort of grew up on his Five Modern Fundamentals of Golf," said Miller. "I studied his every move and analysed his career. Never has there been a golfer who influenced the swing more than Ben Hogan. I still study his book as if it's true scripture.
"He was an amazing guy. Single-minded, maybe almost to a fault. He may be the best player who ever lived. We're going to miss him a lot," said Miller.

"We were friends," said Lee Trevino. "I had something I cherished more than anything -- I had an open invitation to come and play with him any time I wanted to. I used to test all of his golf clubs and everything else that he had. He was the best who ever played."
Ill with colon cancer and Alzheimer's, Hogan, never gregarious, had been a virtual recluse in recent years.
Arnold Palmer recalled that he had not seen Hogan in the last few years before his death. "I was certainly sorry to hear it. I played some golf with Ben over the years and had some fun doing it.
"I certainly enjoyed watching him compete when I was younger. He was, as they say, pretty much a machine. We've lost another good one," said Palmer.
At the Greater Hartford Open, each of the tournament leaders spoke of Hogan.

"It's a great loss," said Brandel Chamblee. "I just hope he got to watch Justin Leonard win the British Open last week. I grew up in Irving (Texas) and got to go watch him hit balls and met him when I played at Colonial in 1983 as an amateur. He inspired all of us."
Leonard, who plays Hogan equipment, lives in Dallas not far from Hogan's home in Ft. Worth, and met him several times.

"It's not new that Mr Hogan is a legend," said Leonard. "He set the standard in dedication to excellence that we can only hope to emulate. I take great pleasure in my association with a company that bears his name and I aspire to uphold the standards that Mr Hogan set throughout his life," said Leonard.
Lanny Wadkins played frequently with Hogan over the past 15 years. "He was a delight to play with, and he could still play. He always used to play me straight up, I never gave him any strokes.
"I think his reputation was wrong. He was just shy off the course, though very competitive once he was on the course," said Wadkins in Hartford.

Ben Crenshaw, a fellow Texan and a historian of the game, said: "For as long as the game is played, the name Ben Hogan will always have a unique fascination for all true golfers, as well as commanding the deepest respect.

"No one ever played the game like Mr Hogan and no human has ever come as close to controlling the golf ball as perfectly as he did. He was relentless in his pursuit of perfection. Ben Hogan defined the inner will that lives within us. The Hawk's shadow will be felt upon the game forever."
